Battle of Zama. In 202 BC near Zama in North Africa, the Roman general Scipio Africanus decisively defeated Hannibal on African soil. The victory ended the Second Punic War and confirmed Rome as the Mediterranean's supreme power.

Scipio commanded approximately 30,000 Roman and allied troops, while Hannibal fielded roughly 40,000, including Numidian cavalry. Hannibal had never been defeated in direct battle, but Scipio had studied his methods and devised a tactical response.

Scipio understood Hannibal's traditional tactic of using war elephants as shock weapons. He spaced his legions to allow the Carthaginian elephants to pass through harmlessly, depriving Hannibal of his opening advantage. The strategy worked perfectly.

Hannibal's cavalry, normally a decisive arm, was neutralized when Massinissa's Numidian riders, allied with Rome, attacked the Carthaginian horse and routed them. Without their cavalry protection, Hannibal's flanks became vulnerable.

The resulting infantry clash brought together two great commanders, but the outcome was decided by Roman discipline and superior training. Hannibal's army was routed despite their numbers. Hannibal himself escaped the field but recognized Carthage's doom. He fled to Asia Minor rather than face capture.

Carthage sued for peace, ceding Spain to Rome, paying heavy indemnities, and sinking into long decline while Rome ascended to supreme power. Scipio Africanus had achieved what years of war could not accomplish. Hannibal, the undefeated general whose genius had brought Rome to the brink at Cannae, suffered his only great defeat at Zama. The Second Punic War was conclusively resolved in Rome's favor, and Carthage's glory was extinguished by the aftermath of Zama's crushing blow.
